```{=html}
<form class="book-practice" id="quiz-p05" data-practice-set="P05" novalidate>
<p id="quiz-p05-instructions">Choose one answer for each of the 10 questions. Complete the set, then select <strong>Check answers</strong> to see your score and explanations. Each question is worth one point.</p>
<noscript><p>For a self-check without JavaScript, record your choices, then open the answer key below.</p></noscript>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-01" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">1.</span> A reader correctly explains a proposal but rejects it because its costs conflict with her priorities. Which conclusion follows?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-01-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-01-a" name="p05-01" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> A clearer font would necessarily resolve the dispute.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-01-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-01-b" name="p05-01" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Rejection proves the proposal was not understood.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-01-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-01-c" name="p05-01" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> The reader&#x27;s priorities must be factually mistaken.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-01-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-01-d" name="p05-01" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Understanding the message does not require agreeing with it.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-01-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-01-e" name="p05-01" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Agreement can be established by repeating the same words.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-01-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-02" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">2.</span> A presentation opens with one moving patient story and then claims a treatment usually works. What evidence is missing for the frequency claim?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-02-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-02-a" name="p05-02" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Several quotations from the same patient</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-02-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-02-b" name="p05-02" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> A shorter name for the treatment</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-02-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-02-c" name="p05-02" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Representative outcome data for comparable patients</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-02-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-02-d" name="p05-02" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> A photograph of the presenter</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-02-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-02-e" name="p05-02" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> A more dramatic ending to the same story</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-02-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-03" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">3.</span> A manager says a pilot is optional but uses a threatening tone and implies refusal will be remembered. Which redesign best preserves meaningful choice?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-03-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-03-a" name="p05-03" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Replace the threatening words while preserving the penalty.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-03-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-03-b" name="p05-03" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Keep the implied penalty but add the word voluntary twice.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-03-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-03-c" name="p05-03" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Count quiet agreement as informed acceptance.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-03-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-03-d" name="p05-03" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Remove refusal penalties and explain the options without pressure.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-03-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-03-e" name="p05-03" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Offer more promotional stories without explaining refusal.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-03-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-04" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">4.</span> A story increases sympathy for a proposal&#x27;s beneficiary, but the audience still worries about funding. What is the most useful next step?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-04-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-04-a" name="p05-04" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Treat sympathy as proof that the funding plan is feasible.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-04-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-04-b" name="p05-04" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Repeat the story until the funding question is no longer raised.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-04-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-04-c" name="p05-04" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Address the funding concern with evidence while retaining the story&#x27;s concrete perspective.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-04-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-04-d" name="p05-04" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Label the question a lack of empathy.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-04-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-04-e" name="p05-04" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Omit all cost information to preserve the story&#x27;s impact.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-04-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-05" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">5.</span> A colleague says a schedule change made her feel disregarded. Which response best checks understanding before proposing a fix?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-05-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-05-a" name="p05-05" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> “The schedule is efficient, so there is no problem.”</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-05-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-05-b" name="p05-05" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> “I know exactly how you feel, so let us move on.”</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-05-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-05-c" name="p05-05" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> “You should use the calendar more carefully.”</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-05-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-05-d" name="p05-05" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> “Everyone feels that way about schedules.”</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-05-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-05-e" name="p05-05" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> “Was being excluded the main concern, or have I misunderstood?”</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-05-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-06" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">6.</span> A brief follows the STORY drafting framework and is easy for readers to summarize, but omits uncertainty that could change the recommended action. What revision best completes the message?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-06-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-06-a" name="p05-06" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Add another story illustrating the preferred outcome.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-06-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-06-b" name="p05-06" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Keep the clear structure and add the uncertain assumption and its decision implications.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-06-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-06-c" name="p05-06" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Treat accurate paraphrasing as proof that the recommendation is correct.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-06-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-06-d" name="p05-06" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Remove the structure and retain only the central recommendation.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-06-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-06-e" name="p05-06" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Describe the framework as validation of the underlying evidence.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-06-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-07" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">7.</span> Two messages are randomly assigned. The study detects higher perceived credibility for one message but no reliable differences in comprehension or uptake. What result should the report state?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-07-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-07-a" name="p05-07" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> The message established the underlying claim&#x27;s truth.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-07-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-07-b" name="p05-07" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> The audience understood the message better.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-07-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-07-c" name="p05-07" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> The message improved actual follow-through.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-07-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-07-d" name="p05-07" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> The message lowered all resistance mechanisms.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-07-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-07-e" name="p05-07" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> The detected difference concerns perceived credibility.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-07-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-08" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">8.</span> Two colleagues agree that a missed handoff was caused by an omitted message, but one still feels publicly humiliated by the accusation. What remains to be addressed?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-08-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-08-a" name="p05-08" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> An instruction to treat shared understanding as forgiveness</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-08-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-08-b" name="p05-08" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Only a second statistical test of the same message log</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-08-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-08-c" name="p05-08" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A stronger accusation to ensure future compliance</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-08-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-08-d" name="p05-08" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Repair of the unfair public account and its relational impact</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-08-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-08-e" name="p05-08" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Proof that the harmed colleague has no emotions</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-08-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-09" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">9.</span> A training advertisement features a top performer whose income doubled after attending. There is no comparison group, and attendees selected themselves. Which revised claim best fits the evidence?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-09-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-09-a" name="p05-09" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Income doubled afterward; the training&#x27;s causal contribution remains unknown.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-09-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-09-b" name="p05-09" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Training caused this person&#x27;s full income increase.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-09-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-09-c" name="p05-09" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Self-selection proves that the training had zero effect.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-09-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-09-d" name="p05-09" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Training doubled income for a typical attendee.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-09-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-09-e" name="p05-09" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> The case establishes the expected gain for a new applicant.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-09-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-10" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">10.</span> Staff accurately explain a proposed workflow, believe it could work, but object that it removes professional discretion. Which response most directly addresses the remaining disagreement?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-10-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-10-a" name="p05-10" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Add another technical success story.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-10-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-10-b" name="p05-10" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Interpret the objection as evidence of deficient listening.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-10-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-10-c" name="p05-10" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Repeat the instructions more slowly.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-10-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-10-d" name="p05-10" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Negotiate which decisions require discretion and revise those boundaries.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-10-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-10-e" name="p05-10" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Test whether staff can recall the platform&#x27;s name.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-10-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<div class="practice-controls"><p class="practice-progress" aria-live="polite">0 of 10 answered</p>
<button class="practice-submit" type="submit" disabled>Check answers</button>
<button class="practice-retry" type="button" hidden>Try again</button></div>
<p class="practice-score" role="status" tabindex="-1" hidden></p>
<details class="practice-key" id="answers-p05"><summary>Answers and explanations</summary><ol class="practice-answer-list">
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p05-01"><h3>Question 1: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. A clearer font would necessarily resolve the dispute. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The obstacle is a substantive cost–priority conflict.</dd>
<dt>B. Rejection proves the proposal was not understood. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The reader has demonstrated understanding.</dd>
<dt>C. The reader&#x27;s priorities must be factually mistaken. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Values are not shown to be erroneous by disagreement alone.</dd>
<dt>D. Understanding the message does not require agreeing with it. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Grounding and persuasion are different accomplishments.</dd>
<dt>E. Agreement can be established by repeating the same words. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Repetition need not change the underlying trade-off.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/30-persuasion.html">Chapter 30</a> · <a href="../chapters/33-communication.html">Chapter 33</a>. <a href="#p05-01">Back to question 1</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p05-02"><h3>Question 2: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Several quotations from the same patient <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Repeated testimony from one case remains one case.</dd>
<dt>B. A shorter name for the treatment <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Naming does not establish effectiveness.</dd>
<dt>C. Representative outcome data for comparable patients <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>One case does not establish how commonly recovery occurs.</dd>
<dt>D. A photograph of the presenter <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Appearance does not supply outcome evidence.</dd>
<dt>E. A more dramatic ending to the same story <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Drama does not identify an outcome rate.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/31-storytelling.html">Chapter 31</a> · <a href="../chapters/32-message-design.html">Chapter 32</a>. <a href="#p05-02">Back to question 2</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p05-03"><h3>Question 3: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Replace the threatening words while preserving the penalty. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Practical freedom remains compromised.</dd>
<dt>B. Keep the implied penalty but add the word voluntary twice. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Labels cannot cancel coercive consequences.</dd>
<dt>C. Count quiet agreement as informed acceptance. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Silence may reflect pressure rather than support.</dd>
<dt>D. Remove refusal penalties and explain the options without pressure. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Both the practical consequences and delivery should support autonomy.</dd>
<dt>E. Offer more promotional stories without explaining refusal. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Stories do not resolve the choice constraint.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/30-persuasion.html">Chapter 30</a> · <a href="../chapters/32-message-design.html">Chapter 32</a>. <a href="#p05-03">Back to question 3</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p05-04"><h3>Question 4: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Treat sympathy as proof that the funding plan is feasible. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Emotional response does not establish feasibility.</dd>
<dt>B. Repeat the story until the funding question is no longer raised. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Repetition avoids the decision-relevant concern.</dd>
<dt>C. Address the funding concern with evidence while retaining the story&#x27;s concrete perspective. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Emotional engagement and the unresolved substantive objection need different support.</dd>
<dt>D. Label the question a lack of empathy. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This treats legitimate scrutiny as a character defect.</dd>
<dt>E. Omit all cost information to preserve the story&#x27;s impact. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>That undermines informed evaluation.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/30-persuasion.html">Chapter 30</a> · <a href="../chapters/31-storytelling.html">Chapter 31</a>. <a href="#p05-04">Back to question 4</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p05-05"><h3>Question 5: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. “The schedule is efficient, so there is no problem.” <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Efficiency does not resolve the relational concern.</dd>
<dt>B. “I know exactly how you feel, so let us move on.” <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Certainty closes the opportunity to correct your understanding.</dd>
<dt>C. “You should use the calendar more carefully.” <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Advice arrives before checking what mattered.</dd>
<dt>D. “Everyone feels that way about schedules.” <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Generalization replaces the colleague&#x27;s specific meaning.</dd>
<dt>E. “Was being excluded the main concern, or have I misunderstood?” <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>A tentative paraphrase invites correction of the inferred concern.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/33-communication.html">Chapter 33</a> · <a href="../chapters/34-connection.html">Chapter 34</a>. <a href="#p05-05">Back to question 5</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p05-06"><h3>Question 6: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Add another story illustrating the preferred outcome. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Illustration does not reveal the consequential uncertainty.</dd>
<dt>B. Keep the clear structure and add the uncertain assumption and its decision implications. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>A drafting aid organizes communication; it does not replace evidence or uncertainty checks.</dd>
<dt>C. Treat accurate paraphrasing as proof that the recommendation is correct. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Understanding does not establish evidential adequacy.</dd>
<dt>D. Remove the structure and retain only the central recommendation. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This neither preserves clarity nor supplies the missing assumption.</dd>
<dt>E. Describe the framework as validation of the underlying evidence. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A communication framework is not a research design.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/32-message-design.html">Chapter 32</a> · <a href="../chapters/33-communication.html">Chapter 33</a>. <a href="#p05-06">Back to question 6</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p05-07"><h3>Question 7: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. The message established the underlying claim&#x27;s truth. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Perceived credibility is not external verification.</dd>
<dt>B. The audience understood the message better. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>No reliable improvement in comprehension was detected.</dd>
<dt>C. The message improved actual follow-through. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>No reliable improvement in uptake was detected.</dd>
<dt>D. The message lowered all resistance mechanisms. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A single rating does not measure every mechanism.</dd>
<dt>E. The detected difference concerns perceived credibility. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The reported effect should match the measured outcome that changed.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/30-persuasion.html">Chapter 30</a> · <a href="../chapters/32-message-design.html">Chapter 32</a>. <a href="#p05-07">Back to question 7</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p05-08"><h3>Question 8: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. An instruction to treat shared understanding as forgiveness <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Understanding does not obligate forgiveness.</dd>
<dt>B. Only a second statistical test of the same message log <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The remaining issue is not uncertainty about the cause.</dd>
<dt>C. A stronger accusation to ensure future compliance <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This would intensify the identified harm.</dd>
<dt>D. Repair of the unfair public account and its relational impact <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Agreement on facts does not by itself repair the harm.</dd>
<dt>E. Proof that the harmed colleague has no emotions <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Emotions can identify a real consequence needing attention.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/33-communication.html">Chapter 33</a> · <a href="../chapters/34-connection.html">Chapter 34</a>. <a href="#p05-08">Back to question 8</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="0" data-question="p05-09"><h3>Question 9: A</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Income doubled afterward; the training&#x27;s causal contribution remains unknown. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Selection and other changes prevent causal attribution from the story alone.</dd>
<dt>B. Training caused this person&#x27;s full income increase. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>No counterfactual isolates that causal contribution.</dd>
<dt>C. Self-selection proves that the training had zero effect. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Failure to identify an effect is not proof of no effect.</dd>
<dt>D. Training doubled income for a typical attendee. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The selected case does not estimate a typical outcome.</dd>
<dt>E. The case establishes the expected gain for a new applicant. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Transport to new applicants is unsupported.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/31-storytelling.html">Chapter 31</a> · <a href="../chapters/32-message-design.html">Chapter 32</a>. <a href="#p05-09">Back to question 9</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p05-10"><h3>Question 10: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Add another technical success story. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>They already accept its potential feasibility.</dd>
<dt>B. Interpret the objection as evidence of deficient listening. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Accurate explanation shows that understanding is present.</dd>
<dt>C. Repeat the instructions more slowly. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Staff already understand the procedure.</dd>
<dt>D. Negotiate which decisions require discretion and revise those boundaries. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The unresolved issue is value and control, not basic comprehension or feasibility.</dd>
<dt>E. Test whether staff can recall the platform&#x27;s name. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Name recall does not address discretion.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/30-persuasion.html">Chapter 30</a> · <a href="../chapters/33-communication.html">Chapter 33</a> · <a href="../chapters/34-connection.html">Chapter 34</a>. <a href="#p05-10">Back to question 10</a></p></li>
</ol></details></form>
<script src="../assets/practice.js" defer></script>
```
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="epub"}
Choose one answer (A–E) for each of the 10 questions. Record all your choices before following the link to the answer key. Each question is worth one point.

::: {#p05-01 .practice-question}
**Question 1.** A reader correctly explains a proposal but rejects it because its costs conflict with her priorities. Which conclusion follows?

A) A clearer font would necessarily resolve the dispute.
B) Rejection proves the proposal was not understood.
C) The reader's priorities must be factually mistaken.
D) Understanding the message does not require agreeing with it.
E) Agreement can be established by repeating the same words.

:::

::: {#p05-02 .practice-question}
**Question 2.** A presentation opens with one moving patient story and then claims a treatment usually works. What evidence is missing for the frequency claim?

A) Several quotations from the same patient
B) A shorter name for the treatment
C) Representative outcome data for comparable patients
D) A photograph of the presenter
E) A more dramatic ending to the same story

:::

::: {#p05-03 .practice-question}
**Question 3.** A manager says a pilot is optional but uses a threatening tone and implies refusal will be remembered. Which redesign best preserves meaningful choice?

A) Replace the threatening words while preserving the penalty.
B) Keep the implied penalty but add the word voluntary twice.
C) Count quiet agreement as informed acceptance.
D) Remove refusal penalties and explain the options without pressure.
E) Offer more promotional stories without explaining refusal.

:::

::: {#p05-04 .practice-question}
**Question 4.** A story increases sympathy for a proposal's beneficiary, but the audience still worries about funding. What is the most useful next step?

A) Treat sympathy as proof that the funding plan is feasible.
B) Repeat the story until the funding question is no longer raised.
C) Address the funding concern with evidence while retaining the story's concrete perspective.
D) Label the question a lack of empathy.
E) Omit all cost information to preserve the story's impact.

:::

::: {#p05-05 .practice-question}
**Question 5.** A colleague says a schedule change made her feel disregarded. Which response best checks understanding before proposing a fix?

A) “The schedule is efficient, so there is no problem.”
B) “I know exactly how you feel, so let us move on.”
C) “You should use the calendar more carefully.”
D) “Everyone feels that way about schedules.”
E) “Was being excluded the main concern, or have I misunderstood?”

:::

::: {#p05-06 .practice-question}
**Question 6.** A brief follows the STORY drafting framework and is easy for readers to summarize, but omits uncertainty that could change the recommended action. What revision best completes the message?

A) Add another story illustrating the preferred outcome.
B) Keep the clear structure and add the uncertain assumption and its decision implications.
C) Treat accurate paraphrasing as proof that the recommendation is correct.
D) Remove the structure and retain only the central recommendation.
E) Describe the framework as validation of the underlying evidence.

:::

::: {#p05-07 .practice-question}
**Question 7.** Two messages are randomly assigned. The study detects higher perceived credibility for one message but no reliable differences in comprehension or uptake. What result should the report state?

A) The message established the underlying claim's truth.
B) The audience understood the message better.
C) The message improved actual follow-through.
D) The message lowered all resistance mechanisms.
E) The detected difference concerns perceived credibility.

:::

::: {#p05-08 .practice-question}
**Question 8.** Two colleagues agree that a missed handoff was caused by an omitted message, but one still feels publicly humiliated by the accusation. What remains to be addressed?

A) An instruction to treat shared understanding as forgiveness
B) Only a second statistical test of the same message log
C) A stronger accusation to ensure future compliance
D) Repair of the unfair public account and its relational impact
E) Proof that the harmed colleague has no emotions

:::

::: {#p05-09 .practice-question}
**Question 9.** A training advertisement features a top performer whose income doubled after attending. There is no comparison group, and attendees selected themselves. Which revised claim best fits the evidence?

A) Income doubled afterward; the training's causal contribution remains unknown.
B) Training caused this person's full income increase.
C) Self-selection proves that the training had zero effect.
D) Training doubled income for a typical attendee.
E) The case establishes the expected gain for a new applicant.

:::

::: {#p05-10 .practice-question}
**Question 10.** Staff accurately explain a proposed workflow, believe it could work, but object that it removes professional discretion. Which response most directly addresses the remaining disagreement?

A) Add another technical success story.
B) Interpret the objection as evidence of deficient listening.
C) Repeat the instructions more slowly.
D) Negotiate which decisions require discretion and revise those boundaries.
E) Test whether staff can recall the platform's name.

:::

[Finished the set? Check the answers and explanations.](#answers-p05)

::: {#answers-p05 .practice-answer-key}
**Answers and explanations**

Count one point for each correct answer, then review the explanations for any alternatives you considered.

**Question 1: D.**

- **A. A clearer font would necessarily resolve the dispute. (Incorrect)** The obstacle is a substantive cost–priority conflict.
- **B. Rejection proves the proposal was not understood. (Incorrect)** The reader has demonstrated understanding.
- **C. The reader's priorities must be factually mistaken. (Incorrect)** Values are not shown to be erroneous by disagreement alone.
- **D. Understanding the message does not require agreeing with it. (Correct)** Grounding and persuasion are different accomplishments.
- **E. Agreement can be established by repeating the same words. (Incorrect)** Repetition need not change the underlying trade-off.

Review: [Chapter 30](../chapters/30-persuasion.qmd) · [Chapter 33](../chapters/33-communication.qmd). [Back to question 1](#p05-01).

**Question 2: C.**

- **A. Several quotations from the same patient (Incorrect)** Repeated testimony from one case remains one case.
- **B. A shorter name for the treatment (Incorrect)** Naming does not establish effectiveness.
- **C. Representative outcome data for comparable patients (Correct)** One case does not establish how commonly recovery occurs.
- **D. A photograph of the presenter (Incorrect)** Appearance does not supply outcome evidence.
- **E. A more dramatic ending to the same story (Incorrect)** Drama does not identify an outcome rate.

Review: [Chapter 31](../chapters/31-storytelling.qmd) · [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 2](#p05-02).

**Question 3: D.**

- **A. Replace the threatening words while preserving the penalty. (Incorrect)** Practical freedom remains compromised.
- **B. Keep the implied penalty but add the word voluntary twice. (Incorrect)** Labels cannot cancel coercive consequences.
- **C. Count quiet agreement as informed acceptance. (Incorrect)** Silence may reflect pressure rather than support.
- **D. Remove refusal penalties and explain the options without pressure. (Correct)** Both the practical consequences and delivery should support autonomy.
- **E. Offer more promotional stories without explaining refusal. (Incorrect)** Stories do not resolve the choice constraint.

Review: [Chapter 30](../chapters/30-persuasion.qmd) · [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 3](#p05-03).

**Question 4: C.**

- **A. Treat sympathy as proof that the funding plan is feasible. (Incorrect)** Emotional response does not establish feasibility.
- **B. Repeat the story until the funding question is no longer raised. (Incorrect)** Repetition avoids the decision-relevant concern.
- **C. Address the funding concern with evidence while retaining the story's concrete perspective. (Correct)** Emotional engagement and the unresolved substantive objection need different support.
- **D. Label the question a lack of empathy. (Incorrect)** This treats legitimate scrutiny as a character defect.
- **E. Omit all cost information to preserve the story's impact. (Incorrect)** That undermines informed evaluation.

Review: [Chapter 30](../chapters/30-persuasion.qmd) · [Chapter 31](../chapters/31-storytelling.qmd). [Back to question 4](#p05-04).

**Question 5: E.**

- **A. “The schedule is efficient, so there is no problem.” (Incorrect)** Efficiency does not resolve the relational concern.
- **B. “I know exactly how you feel, so let us move on.” (Incorrect)** Certainty closes the opportunity to correct your understanding.
- **C. “You should use the calendar more carefully.” (Incorrect)** Advice arrives before checking what mattered.
- **D. “Everyone feels that way about schedules.” (Incorrect)** Generalization replaces the colleague's specific meaning.
- **E. “Was being excluded the main concern, or have I misunderstood?” (Correct)** A tentative paraphrase invites correction of the inferred concern.

Review: [Chapter 33](../chapters/33-communication.qmd) · [Chapter 34](../chapters/34-connection.qmd). [Back to question 5](#p05-05).

**Question 6: B.**

- **A. Add another story illustrating the preferred outcome. (Incorrect)** Illustration does not reveal the consequential uncertainty.
- **B. Keep the clear structure and add the uncertain assumption and its decision implications. (Correct)** A drafting aid organizes communication; it does not replace evidence or uncertainty checks.
- **C. Treat accurate paraphrasing as proof that the recommendation is correct. (Incorrect)** Understanding does not establish evidential adequacy.
- **D. Remove the structure and retain only the central recommendation. (Incorrect)** This neither preserves clarity nor supplies the missing assumption.
- **E. Describe the framework as validation of the underlying evidence. (Incorrect)** A communication framework is not a research design.

Review: [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd) · [Chapter 33](../chapters/33-communication.qmd). [Back to question 6](#p05-06).

**Question 7: E.**

- **A. The message established the underlying claim's truth. (Incorrect)** Perceived credibility is not external verification.
- **B. The audience understood the message better. (Incorrect)** No reliable improvement in comprehension was detected.
- **C. The message improved actual follow-through. (Incorrect)** No reliable improvement in uptake was detected.
- **D. The message lowered all resistance mechanisms. (Incorrect)** A single rating does not measure every mechanism.
- **E. The detected difference concerns perceived credibility. (Correct)** The reported effect should match the measured outcome that changed.

Review: [Chapter 30](../chapters/30-persuasion.qmd) · [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 7](#p05-07).

**Question 8: D.**

- **A. An instruction to treat shared understanding as forgiveness (Incorrect)** Understanding does not obligate forgiveness.
- **B. Only a second statistical test of the same message log (Incorrect)** The remaining issue is not uncertainty about the cause.
- **C. A stronger accusation to ensure future compliance (Incorrect)** This would intensify the identified harm.
- **D. Repair of the unfair public account and its relational impact (Correct)** Agreement on facts does not by itself repair the harm.
- **E. Proof that the harmed colleague has no emotions (Incorrect)** Emotions can identify a real consequence needing attention.

Review: [Chapter 33](../chapters/33-communication.qmd) · [Chapter 34](../chapters/34-connection.qmd). [Back to question 8](#p05-08).

**Question 9: A.**

- **A. Income doubled afterward; the training's causal contribution remains unknown. (Correct)** Selection and other changes prevent causal attribution from the story alone.
- **B. Training caused this person's full income increase. (Incorrect)** No counterfactual isolates that causal contribution.
- **C. Self-selection proves that the training had zero effect. (Incorrect)** Failure to identify an effect is not proof of no effect.
- **D. Training doubled income for a typical attendee. (Incorrect)** The selected case does not estimate a typical outcome.
- **E. The case establishes the expected gain for a new applicant. (Incorrect)** Transport to new applicants is unsupported.

Review: [Chapter 31](../chapters/31-storytelling.qmd) · [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 9](#p05-09).

**Question 10: D.**

- **A. Add another technical success story. (Incorrect)** They already accept its potential feasibility.
- **B. Interpret the objection as evidence of deficient listening. (Incorrect)** Accurate explanation shows that understanding is present.
- **C. Repeat the instructions more slowly. (Incorrect)** Staff already understand the procedure.
- **D. Negotiate which decisions require discretion and revise those boundaries. (Correct)** The unresolved issue is value and control, not basic comprehension or feasibility.
- **E. Test whether staff can recall the platform's name. (Incorrect)** Name recall does not address discretion.

Review: [Chapter 30](../chapters/30-persuasion.qmd) · [Chapter 33](../chapters/33-communication.qmd) · [Chapter 34](../chapters/34-connection.qmd). [Back to question 10](#p05-10).

:::
